assets.title: 19% reply rate: the outreach wasn't cold, it was specific
assets.body:
A 19% reply rate on cold email sounds fake. It wasn't cold.

What I actually did:

1. Opened a blank spreadsheet.
2. Listed 200 companies that had publicly complained about the exact problem I solved. Public complaints only — their words, on the record.
3. Wrote 200 emails that each quoted their own complaint back to them.

That's it. No sequence tool, no 7-touch cadence, no personalisation tokens.

The reply rate was ~19%, and that number isn't a hack. It's just what happens when the recipient can tell the email could not have been sent to anyone else.

"Cold" is not a channel problem. It's a specificity problem. Most cold email fails because it would still make sense if you swapped the company name — and everyone can feel that.

40 of those 200 became customers.
rationale: Score 81, but the payoff is a numbered mechanism plus a reply-rate stat — that reads as a process, not a visual, so X beats another vertical cut.
Deliberately paired with the 38s Shorts cut of the same span: the Short carries the story, this carries the 19% analysis, so they reinforce rather than duplicate.
Matches Alex's 'practical' brief — a founder can execute all three steps without buying anything.

assets.title: Distribution vs. advertising: the compounding test
assets.body:
Distribution is not a channel. It's a compounding loop.

The test is one question: does every customer you land make the next one cheaper to reach?

If yes, that's distribution.
If no, that's advertising. Advertising is fine — but price it honestly. It stops the day you stop paying.

Most early founders say "we're figuring out distribution" when they mean "we're buying attention." Those are different companies with different unit economics.

Run the test on your own numbers before your next channel experiment.
rationale: Score 76 and the shape is a definition plus a one-question test — framework-shaped content that survives as text and loses nothing without video.
X was in the suggested set and this is the kind of contrarian-but-defensible claim that gets quote-tweeted by founders, which is Alex's audience.
Kept short on purpose: the mechanic that proves it (the footer loop) is a separate, weaker moment and is being held back for verification rather than padded in here.

assets.title: The question your price is training buyers to ask
assets.body:
When I moved from $19 to $59, the questions changed.

At $19: "Is there a free plan?"
At $59: "What does onboarding look like?"

Same product. Same week. Different buyer posture.

Price isn't just what you capture — it's the instruction you hand the buyer about how seriously to take you. A cheap price invites people to evaluate whether to pay at all. A real price invites them to evaluate whether it will work.

If every sales call opens with a discount question, that's not a sales problem.
rationale: Score 72 — mid-tier, but the before/after quote pair is unusually clean and lands better as read text than as a talking-head clip.
Sits between the pricing Short and the pricing newsletter as the mid-week connective post; different angle (buyer behaviour) so it doesn't repeat the 3x-price claim.
No motivational framing, just the observed change in question type — consistent with Alex's stated 'avoid generic motivational language'.

assets.title: $19 felt safe. That was the problem.
assets.body:
SUBJECT: $19 felt safe. That was the problem.
PREVIEW: What a low price actually signals to your first ten customers.

—

I launched at $19/month because it felt safe.

It wasn't safe. It was a signal, and the signal was: this is a toy.

Here's the sequence, with real numbers:

**$19 — the toy price**
I picked it by looking at what felt uncomfortable to charge and then going one step below that. That's not pricing, that's flinching. Every inbound conversation started with some version of "is there a free tier?" — because I'd already told them the product was worth roughly nothing.

**$59 — the conversation flips**
Same product, same week. The questions changed to "what does onboarding look like?" Buyers stopped negotiating whether to pay and started planning how to use it. I hadn't added a feature. I'd removed an excuse.

**3x — and zero churn**
When I tripled the price, I lost exactly zero customers. Not because I'm a great salesperson. Because of something I misunderstood for the whole first month:

Your first ten customers are not buying software. They're buying a fix for a problem that is already costing them more than your price tag.

If the problem burns $4,000 a month of someone's time, $19 and $59 are the same number to them. The gap between those two prices only exists in your head. The only person a low price protects is the founder.

**What to do this week**
1. Write down what the problem costs your customer per month. Get an actual figure from an actual customer — don't estimate it.
2. Compare it to your price. If your price is under 5% of that number, you are not priced, you are apologising.
3. Raise the price for new customers only. Grandfather the existing ones. You now have a clean test with no downside.
4. Track the first question new prospects ask. That's your real pricing signal, faster than any conversion number.

One caveat, so this isn't advice-shaped noise: this held for me at 40 customers solving one sharply defined problem. If you're selling something broad to a market that hasn't named the pain yet, a higher price won't rescue that. Fix the specificity first.

— Alex

P.S. The full 30-day build video is here, pricing section starts at 8:42.
rationale: Three pricing moments (74, 66, 72) cover one continuous arc — $19 to $59 to 3x — and none of them stands alone at Short length. Assembled, they form the newsletter's natural narrative spine.
m_cheap_pricing_changes_th (66) is a duplicate span and transcript of m_19_signalled_a_toy (74); it produced no separate asset and is absorbed here rather than shipped twice.
Newsletter is where Alex's 'educational' register has room for the caveat at the end — the honest boundary condition that would be cut from a 35-second Short and would read as hedging on X.

DESCRIPTION
I built and shipped a SaaS product in 30 days. This is the unedited version of what actually moved the numbers — not the montage.

Inside:
• How I got the first 40 customers from a 200-row spreadsheet and zero ad spend, at a ~19% reply rate
• Why I started at $19, why that was a mistake, and what happened when I tripled the price
• The exact moment buyer questions changed from "is there a free plan?" to "what does onboarding look like?"
• The difference between distribution and advertising, and the one question that tells you which you have
• The footer loop that was driving roughly a third of signups by week four

Built for early-stage founders who need something to do on Monday, not something to feel good about on Sunday.

Chapters are below. Pricing section starts at 8:42.

nextRecommendation.title: The five-line email I sent when I tripled my price
nextRecommendation.format: First-person written case study, same format and channel as the winner. 800–1,200 words, single narrative, with the actual email reproduced in full as the centrepiece artifact. Publish within 10 days while the 1,240 new subscribers are still warm.
nextRecommendation.reason: The winner proved two things independently: the topic (pricing) pulls clicks, and the open-loop hook holds attention. But 81% retention against a 62% baseline tells you something more specific — people stayed because they wanted the mechanism, not the outcome. They already had the outcome in the title. The thing they clicked for was *how*, and the honest read is that a single post can only partly deliver that. This piece pays off the exact question the last one opened, which is the cheapest audience demand you will ever get to serve. Reproducing the actual email is what makes it a new post rather than a rerun: it's an artifact, not a retelling, and artifacts are the part readers screenshot and forward. The title keeps the three mechanics that worked — first person, a specific number, a concrete noun that can't be resolved from the headline — while swapping the promise from result to method, so it reads as a sequel rather than a repeat. Main risk, stated plainly: sequels typically underperform the original because the curiosity gap is narrower, and one 2.3x post is a single data point, not a trend. Expect something between baseline and the winner, not another 94,800. Treat this as the post that converts the new subscribers into readers who trust you on pricing specifically — that's the durable asset here, more than the view count.
evidence: Pricing is the creator's strongest topic and the winner sat directly on it: 94,800 views vs a 41,200 baseline (2.3x)
Retention of 81% vs 62% baseline indicates readers stayed for the unresolved 'how', which this post delivers directly — the demand is already measured, not assumed
CTR 9.1% vs 5.4% baseline came from a hook pattern with three reusable parts (first person, specific number, counterintuitive or concrete payoff); the proposed title preserves all three
1,240 new subscribers arrived via a pricing post and have no other content from this creator on that topic yet — highest-intent segment available, and it decays
Counter-evidence a sceptic should weigh: this is one post, not a validated pattern; sequel posts usually capture less curiosity than the original because the headline gap is smaller

Counter-evidence: it is not separable from this data whether the lift came from the pricing topic or the hook structure — if it was the hook, the same structure applied to distribution or AI tools would test that, and is the better next experiment if this post underperforms
